plain_english: Think about this: you're heading to court. What do you want to defend? What do you want to win? If you want to defend a life that follows nature, you have complete security. You have every advantage. You have no problems. If you want to defend what's actually in your power — what's naturally free — and if you're satisfied with those things, what else matters? Who controls things like that? Who can take them away? If you choose to be humble and honest, who can stop you? If you choose not to be held back or forced into anything, who can make you want something you think you shouldn't want?
original_excerpt: Consider, you who are going into court, what you wish to maintain and what you wish to succeed in. For if you wish to maintain a will conformable to nature, you have every security, every facility, you have no troubles. For if you wish to maintain what is in your own power and is naturally free, and if you are content with these, what else do you care for? For who is the master of such things? Who can take them away? If you choose to be modest and faithful, who shall not allow you to be so? If you choose not to be restrained or compelled, who shall compel you to desire what you think that you ought not to desire?

plain_english: Who can force you to avoid something you don't think you should avoid? But what do you say? The judge might rule against you with something that seems scary. But can he also make you suffer while you're trying to avoid it? How could he do that? When going after things and avoiding things are in your power, what else matters? Let this be your opening. Let this be your story. Let this be your proof. Let this be your victory. Let this be your closing argument. Let this be your applause.
original_excerpt: who shall compel you to avoid what you do not think fit to avoid? But what do you say? The judge will determine against you something that appears formidable; but that you should also suffer in trying to avoid it, how can he do that? When then the pursuit of objects and the avoiding of them are in your power, what else do you care for? Let this be your preface, this your narrative, this your confirmation, this your victory, this your peroration, this your applause (or the approbation which you will receive).

plain_english: That's why Socrates said to someone who told him to prepare for his trial, "Don't you think I've been preparing for this my whole life?" The person asked, "What kind of preparation?" Socrates answered, "I've focused on what was in my control. I've never done anything unjust in my private life or my public life."
original_excerpt: Therefore Socrates said to one who was reminding him to prepare for his trial, Do you not think then that I have been preparing for it all my life? By what kind of preparation? I have maintained that which was in my own power. How then? I have never done anything unjust either in my private or in my public life.

plain_english: But if you want to hold onto externals too — your fragile body, your small possessions, your little reputation — then I advise you to prepare as much as possible right now. Consider both the nature of your judge and your opponent. If you need to beg on your knees, beg on your knees. If you need to cry, cry. If you need to groan, groan. Once you've made what's truly yours subject to external things, then be a slave and don't resist. Don't sometimes choose to be a slave and sometimes not. With your whole mind, be one or the other — either free or enslaved, either educated or ignorant, either a noble fighting cock or a cowardly one. Either endure being beaten until you die, or give up immediately. Don't let yourself take many blows and then surrender anyway. But if these things are shameful, decide right now. Where is the nature of good and evil? It's where truth is. Where truth and nature are, there is wisdom. Where truth is, there is courage where nature is.
original_excerpt: But if you wish to maintain externals also, your poor body, your little property, and your little estimation, I advise you to make from this moment all possible preparation, and then consider both the nature of your judge and your adversary. If it is necessary to embrace his knees, embrace his knees; if to weep, weep; if to groan, groan. For when you have subjected to externals what is your own, then be a slave and do not resist, and do not sometimes choose to be a slave, and sometimes not choose, but with all your mind be one or the other, either free or a slave, either instructed or uninstructed, either a well-bred cock or a mean one, either endure to be beaten until you die or yield at once; and let it not happen to you to receive many stripes and then to yield. But if these things are base, determine immediately. Where is the nature of evil and good? It is where truth is: where truth is and where nature is, there is caution: where truth is, there is courage where nature is.

plain_english: This is why it's ridiculous when someone says, "Give me advice. Tell me what to do." What should I tell you? "Train your mind to handle whatever happens." But that's like someone who can't read saying, "Tell me what to write when someone gives me a name." If I tell him to write "Dion," and then someone else comes and asks him to write "Theon" instead, what happens? What will he write? But if you've practiced writing, you're ready to write anything that's needed. If you haven't practiced, what can I possibly suggest? If circumstances demand something different, what will you say or do? Remember this basic rule and you won't need suggestions. But if you chase after external things, you'll inevitably run around following your master's orders. And who is your master? Whoever controls the things you're trying to get or avoid.
original_excerpt: For this reason also it is ridiculous to say, Suggest something to me (tell me what to do). What should I suggest to you? Well, form my mind so as to accommodate itself to any event. Why that is just the same as if a man who is ignorant of letters should say, Tell me what to write when any name is proposed to me. For if I should tell him to write Dion, and then another should come and propose to him not the name of Dion but that of Theon, what will be done? what will he write? But if you have practised writing, you are also prepared to write (or to do) anything that is required. If you are not, what can I now suggest? For if circumstances require something else, what will you say, or what will you do? Remember then this general precept and you will need no suggestion. But if you gape after externals, you must of necessity ramble up and down in obedience to the will of your master. And who is the master? He who has the power over the things which you seek to gain or try to avoid.
